title: HHS finalizes ‘portion’ of employee layoffs following Supreme Court ruling
summary: Many Health and Human Services workers who got layoff notices in April are now officially separated from the agency, according to an internal email Monday, a week after the Supreme Court said agencies could proceed with reduction-in-force plans.
content:
By Jory Heckman

Many employees who received layoff notices from the Department of Health and Human Services in April are now officially separated from the agency, according to an email that went out Monday afternoon.

In an email obtained by Federal News Network, HHS told employees that the Supreme Court’s ruling on July 8 allows the department to proceed with “a portion” of its reduction-in-force plans.

“Accordingly, you are hereby notified that you are officially separated from HHS at the close of business on July 14, 2025,” the email states. “Thank you for your service to the American people.”

HHS sent RIF notices to 10,000 employees on April 1. Another 10,000 employees left by accepting voluntary separation incentives. Altogether, the department is cutting about 25% of its staff.

HHS employees who received RIF notices in April were scheduled to be officially separated from the agency by June 2. But a preliminary injunction issued in May by a federal judge in San Francisco prevented HHS and many other agencies from proceeding with RIFs and reorganization plans. The Supreme Court’s recent ruling overturned that preliminary injunction.

An HHS spokesperson told Federal News Network that all employees who received RIF notices have been officially separated from the agency, except a narrow group of employees covered by a preliminary injunction issued by a federal judge in Rhode Island, and those who have been reinstated in recent months.

Supreme Court opens door to large-scale federal layoffs

That injunction, issued July 1 by U.S. District Judge Melissa DuBose in Rhode Island is still in place and covers employees at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Food and Drug Administration’s Center for Tobacco Products, the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation, and the Office of Head Start, as well as Head Start employees in regional offices.

Since April, HHS has reinstated some employees across the department, including employees at the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, human resources staff, and acquisition experts within the Office of the Chief Information Officer.

HHS faces other legal challenges over its workforce cuts. A class-action lawsuit in the U.S. Court for the District of Columbia claims the department relied on “hopelessly error-ridden” data when it carried out the mass terminations on April 1.

Federal employees under the Privacy Act can challenge adverse personnel actions based on inaccurate or incomplete records.

A Food and Drug Administration employee who received a termination letter on Monday told Federal News Network that HHS never corrected any of the dates or inaccurate performance ratings from their original RIF notice.

“Statutes state that if a RIF notice contains errors, it needs to be reissued with corrected information and the clock starts over. This has not happened,” the FDA employee said.

The FDA employee said those officially separated from the agency have been shut out of its HR system, and that they have gotten “zero information on severance.”

An employee at the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration said they received a termination letter Monday, despite a “consistent history of outstanding performance ratings,” and their status as a disabled veteran.

“None of it mattered. They don’t even know who they fired,” the SAMHSA employee said.

“The email provides no corrected information, no next steps — nothing,” the employee said.

Supreme Court clears the way for sweeping cuts at Education Department

The National Treasury Employees Union, which represents some HHS employees, said in an email that it will ensure impacted bargaining unit members have legal representation before the Merit Systems Protection Board, either through NTEU or partner organizations.

“We have been working on the best strategies for anticipated member representation at the MSPB for months and will finalize those plans now that separations are occurring,” NTEU wrote.

Appeals to the MSPB must be filed no later than 30 days after the effective date of an employee’s separation.

Administrative judges at MSPB, who adjudicate appeals from federal employees alleging prohibited personnel practices, have seen a flood of new cases land on their docket. Since President Donald Trump took office, the average weekly number of new appeals has risen to roughly 468 — compared with an average of 96 weekly appeals federal employees were filing in the final few months of 2024.

HHS is the third agency to advance its workforce cuts following the Supreme Court’s ruling.

The State Department laid off more than 1,350 employees last Friday. The Education Department will proceed with its plans to lay off nearly 1,400 employees after the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to proceed with its cuts to the department in a ruling Monday.
